utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the Judge. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning -- rather, good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We will have a witness today who will testify by video conference; is that right? Mr. Bakrac, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see now if the videolink is working. Very good. Thank you. Perfect. Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Witness, can you hear us in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please swear under oath that you will tell the truth, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Interpretation] Pardon? Should I read this out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Interpretation] Can I please have the text in Serbian? There is a term here, "pricegnoti [phoen]" which I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I do not know which text you were given. Mr. Registrar, could you please confirm that the witness has a text he can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Interpretation] No, I thought I was supposed to take an oath, but I heard a term which I didn't understand what it meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be able to swear under oath with the text that you have in front of you? With that text, there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Bakrac -- oh, I see the Prosecutor on his feet. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I just wonder whether the formalities of 15 bis perhaps should be put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're absolutely right. Given some exceptional circumstances, since Judge Orie cannot be present today, we will be sitting under Article 15 bis. Thank you very much, Mr. Groome. Mr. Bakrac, it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I commence, may I just note that during proofing this witness told us that he is suffering from a very high eye pressure. Due to this, if he exerts himself too much he suffers from severe headaches. I told him that should something like that arise that he can approach you and ask for a break, and I hope that by doing so I did not exceed my authority. Secondly, I will be doing my best. This is something that we were doing during proofing as well, not to ask the witness to read portions of text. This is very difficult for him, especially if the text is in small print. So I will ask him to read only a limited portion of text so as to avoid this, if you will allow me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Bakrac, and thank you for reminding us that the witness has some eye problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness has to read a text or a document which you would like to show to the Court, it could maybe be done this way. Maybe you could read the relevant passages into the microphone and slowly so that the interpretation can be done because the interpreters, of course, will not have the text. Is that okay with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. You're right. And I will do my best to go through the exercise slowly so as not to create any problems for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Opacic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In order to conduct this direct examination as efficiently as possible, Mr. Opacic, kindly wait for my question to be put to you and do not start answering right away; rather, make a small break after I have finished putting my question to you. Perhaps the Registrar who is with you there can help us. He can signal you when it is that you can start giving your answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, please, for the sake of the record, state your full name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Opacic. Should I give you my date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, I will be putting the questions to you. Kindly tell us the date and place of birth -- your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: The 11th of March, 1964, in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, can you tell us - slowly, please - what sort of schooling have you had?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I completed my primary education in the municipality of Benkovac. Later on I attended the secondary school of internal affairs in Zagreb. These were four years of secondary schooling, and that is the education that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When was it that you graduated from the secondary school of internal affairs in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you get a job somewhere, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, all the student of the secondary school of internal affairs would get a job somewhere with the organs of internal affairs, and I was posted to the police station in Sinj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Until what year did you continue working for the station in Sinj and what were your specific duties?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I worked there from 1983 through to early 1988, and I was a patrol officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic. In 1988 where were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I transferred to the internal affairs organ in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your specific duties in Zadar were and until when you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: My duties in Zadar were also those of a ordinary policeman going on patrol. However, there was also a special unit composed of policemen who were younger than 28 and formed some sort of a special unit. I had attended training for sniper shooting, so I was basically also assigned to that specific unit during my time both in Sinj and Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In addition to the policing, were you training any sort of sports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, in high school I practiced karate and I was one of the best athletes in my secondary school. As I came to Sinj I started training kick-boxing, the contact sports, and then I proceeded on to train classic boxing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you go to any official competitions? Sports competitions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did you compete for the colours of your station in Sinj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, there were police sports games for the region of Dalmatia, and I regularly participated as an athlete, 800 metres racing and so on. I could not participate with my basic sport of kick-boxing because they wouldn't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Until what time did you continue working for the Zadar police station?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I worked there until mid-November 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What happened? Why did you no longer work for the Zadar police station after mid-November 1990?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: When the Croatian Democratic Union came to power, I did not wish to sign an oath of loyalty to them, and I didn't want to wear the symbol of the chequer-board besides, they also admitted people who were civilians, who also used to have a criminal record. They were individuals who we at some point had arrested for brawling, for violent behaviour, for theft and that sort of crime. I refused to work along side such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, while you were a patrolling police officer in Sinj and Zadar, did you receive any sort of citations or awards?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I received an award for the best policeman of the town of Sinj while I was working for the station in Sinj. I received some sort of a vase and a commendation in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know which year was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: 1985 or 1986. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, during your time in Sinj and Zadar, were you accused of any sort of misdemeanor or exceeding your authority or crime?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not held responsible for any crimes or misdemeanors. Rather, in Zadar, in 1990, I was suspended along with 15 other policemen of Serb ethnicity, and we were suspended for the fact that we complained about these individuals with a criminal past having been admitted onto the force, which is something I've just explained to you a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, in November of 1990 you were suspended. Do you know when it was that you were officially dismissed? When it was that your status as policeman for the Zadar station were terminated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, I was kept in the records of the police all the way through to February of 1991, although I left the station in November of 1990 and never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you left the police force in Zadar, where did you go next? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: At first I went to Biljane Gornje which is my native village in the municipality of Benkovac. There was a disco there, and I worked in that disco as a bouncer for about a month. Next, I went to the municipality building in Benkovac where I reported to the president of the municipality, Zekovac [phoen], and I and my brother, Zoran, Cedo Zecevic, and another person, we, all of us, worked there as security guards. Some of us came from Sinj, some from Benkovac, some from Zadar, all of them having left their respective police forces the same way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when road blocks were erected in your area, and if so, who erected them, and did you have any part in that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Road blocks had been erected back in 1990 at a time when the president of the SAO Krajina was Milan Babic. It may have been the month of August. Locals participated in that and I took part in that as well, together with the villages. I was with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, you say that your brother, you, and two more former policemen worked as security guards for Zecevic. Do you know if at some point in 1991 an individual by the name of Captain Dragan came to visit Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I think it was the month of February or March that he came. I wasn't there at the time. I think he was accompanied by Dejan Lucic [phoen], a journalist. The next time there were Lucic, Prika, and Pavic who came to see Zecevic again, and then they talked about Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Zecevic tell you where why Captain Dragan came and what they talked about, and do you know if Zecevic took him anywhere?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I think that Zecevic took him to see Milan Martic. And it was as if he was somebody who had been to different fronts, in Africa. He was introduced as some sort of commando, a person who had been to fronts as a member of the Foreign Legion, a legionnaire. He was a mercenary, simply speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know what they talked about, Captain Dragan, Martic, and Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic. Do you know a person by the name of Dragan Karna?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Dragan Karna is a colleague of mine. We worked together in Sinj for five years at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And in early 1991, do you know where Dragan Karna was? What was his post at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: When he came from Sinj, Dragan Karna came to Knin, and a special unit was formed, the same that we had before in the SUPs which was located in Golubic. It's a youth village where youth work drives had been organised before, and then the huts remained. It was abandoned and this is where the police were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that a special police force was formed. Can you be a bit more specific as to when this special police with Dragan Karna was formed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I think that this was -- it was after the action in Plitvice by the Croatian MUP, but this was there before as well, but it wasn't organised as well as it was after that action. It was done more thoroughly, to have this unit formed of people who were trained, who had gone through training. Mostly the unit consisted of the same policemen who came from Zagreb, Split, Sinj, Zadar, Rijeka, Biograd na Moru, and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, did you join this unit at some point?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I joined the units, if I recall correctly, in late April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, when you say late April 1991, that time that you joined, was it already then that Captain Golubic came to -- Captain Dragan came to Golubic. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, Captain Dragan came to Golubic in May, I think. In the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask now for this video-clip. We also have the transcript, so, if you permit me, I don't want to play this video-clip that we already looked at. I am only going to read slowly to the witness a part of the statement by Dragan Karna from this video so that we can see if this corresponds to the witness's experiences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sure, absolutely, but please first explain to the witness what is it about, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is Exhibit D117.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Opacic, I am now -- Mr. Karna gave a statement about the Golubic unit on television. I am going to read a part of it and I am going to ask you to say whether what is being read to you is actually something that you recall. We're looking at page 2 in the Serbian and in the English. I am slowly going to be begin to read. It's in the middle of the interview where Dragan Karna says: "I will start with 31st of March, 1991. Members of this detachment took part in the combat in Plitvice. On the 2nd of May, 1991, an attack on the Kijevo police station was launched. On May 3rd, 1991, members of the detachment disarmed the citizens of Croat ethnicity in Vrhpolje and Potkolje."

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Potkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "These citizens under the guise of the HDZ party carried out arming and prepared to close up the police stations, which they were prevented from doing by the members of this detachment. On this occasion, 38 automatic rifles, Kalashnikov; 68 bombs; and 38 impact rifle grenades were confiscated. On May 6th, 1991, the members of this unit formed the police station in Bratuskovac, which is in the hinterland of Skradinac [phoen]. On the 15th of May, 1991, after the educational centre of Golubic was formed under the leadership of Captain Dragan, the complete unit underwent training. In the course of the training, during the training itself, combat activities were carried out: "Thus the members of the unit were also carrying out combat activities and destroying the Ustasha educational centre in Ljubovo (indiscernible) Korenica." This was an excerpt from the interview by Dragan Karna. According to your recollection, is this correct what Dragan Karna said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I participated in the action to disarm these civilians who were armed with Kalashnikovs in Vrhpolje and Potkonje. And it's true that a police station was formed in Bratiskovci [as interpreted], this is the hinterland of Skradiste [as interpreted]. It's true that Captain Dragan arrived on the 15th of May to Golubic. And it is also correct that an attack was carried out at the Ljubova police station near Korenica. I don't know what else is stated there. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, what changed in Golubic in this special police unit, if anything did, once Captain Dragan arrived on the 15th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, we thought Captain Dragan was some sort of an expert. But actually, as far as infantry training is concerned, he went through that training in the same way that we all did, and that's what he knew. We were trained to jump out of Land Rovers at the speed of 30 kilometres an hour. Some people fell and hurt themselves. Some people complained to Martic that the training was inappropriate so that Captain Dragan then had a conflict with Martic immediately because of the training, the way it was. I had gone through physical endurance training in Golubic with the members who were in that unit. We were there for 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, when you say "inappropriate" - I am looking at the transcript - when you say that what do you mean by that? Was there anything there that was against the laws and customs of war, something that was inappropriate for civilians, or was it inappropriate in some other way?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It was inappropriate as far as the people who were being trained is concerned. We were not used to jumping out of vehicles; for example, a driver would be driving a Land Rover and you would be forced to jump out while it was going at the speed of 30 to 40 kilometres an hour. People were not used to that and they got hurt. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And those of you who went through police regular training and training in the JNA, did you learn anything new while undergoing this training with Captain Dragan? Something that was not taught during regular police or army training.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I mentioned before that I was a member of a special unit in Sinj and in Zadar, so we did have all of this training before. Everything -- I was a sniper by training in these special units. That was my specialty. I went to a training course for a month which was organised by instructors of the special police forces in Zagreb. The first course of training was in Cakovec, it's a town in northern Croatia. The second training course was in Potkonje, in the area of Lika. And this special unit of ours was well-equipped. We had double uniforms. We were paid more than regular members. We had Hecklers with silencers, machine-guns, sniper rifles. We had chemical tear-gas bombs and other devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Opacic, all of these things that you just told us has to do with the training that you had before war broke out -- this was in Zagreb in the Croatian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, can you please tell me, when Captain Dragan came, did anything change in the position of Mr. Dragan Karna?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, he remained in the post of commander of that unit, even though I had a conflict with Karna because of an attitude towards members of these other police units, from Obrovac, Benkovac. I had a problem with his attitude towards those people, but we worked it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that you spent 20 days in training. Did I understand you correctly, to be counting these 20 days from the point in time when Captain Dragan came?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, 20 days because Captain Dragan saw that we knew all of these things and so there was no need for us to stay there for a long time in training, to waste time with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know how long Captain Dragan was conducting this training in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I think it was until his conflict with Mile Martic. Perhaps this was until July or August. I think it was in July. I cannot remember exactly, but I know that there was a conflict between Martic and him and that Martic expelled him from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell me who sent you to Golubic? How did you get to this unit of Dragan Karna and stay for this training by Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: This was an order by the minister of interior of SAO Krajina. Martic issued an order to all the police stations, such as Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac of the SAO Krajina, to send all of these members who had completed the training, who were younger, who had been working in those police branches to be sent to Knin for the special unit to be formed -- actually, for special units in Golubic which had already been trained and had undergone training.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what you're saying now, is that a decision of Mr. Martic before Captain Dragan came or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: This was his decision that pre-dated the arrival of Captain Dragan. I came to Golubic based on that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know when Captain Dragan came and conducted the training? How long did the people who were going under -- undergoing training keep arriving to Golubic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, there weren't really -- the conditions there weren't all that great. These huts -- the conditions were not great. Everything was outdated and dilapidated. And people really couldn't stay there that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell me, did anybody else come with Captain Dragan to give the training?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: We called him Marko Irac, he came with him. We didn't know his last name. His name was Marko Irac. He was together with Captain Dragan. They went to France together, in Africa. That's what the stories were. He was blonde with freckles, short hair. That's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, when you say "Marko Irac," is he a citizen of Serbia or the former Yugoslavia, or did he come from some other place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, he was a foreigner. He was Irish. They told me that he was from Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic. Can you please tell me, after you completed the training that lasted for 20 days, did you learn anything in this training which you and your colleagues did not know until then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: My colleagues and I knew all of these things already. All the things that were part of the training we already knew. There was no need for us to go through the training at all. There was no point in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell us when it was that you completed your training, approximately, and where you went next?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It was somewhere on the 5th or 6th of June. We went back to the Benkovac police station and resumed our policing duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say your policing duties, do you mean the patrolling duties that you had performed before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That's correct. However, since we were also a special unit - and that was the practice that was continued on from our time in Croatia - whenever we were off duty we had to report our whereabouts to the duty officer so that if an incident emerged or if there was a brawl, if there was an incursion by terrorist groups, we would be able to get activated immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Before we leave Golubic to discuss other issues, tell us, during your time in Golubic did you receive a salary, and if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: We received our pay from the Knin SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know who was responsible for ensuring that this, let's call it camp, at Golubic was properly run in terms of having meals, the necessary equipment, materiel, and assets, if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the ministry -- or, I mean the Ministry of the Interior in Knin and of the government of SAO Krajina. There were also individuals who raised funds. They were like private donations that they would give to the Ministry of the Interior and they would use some of these funds to pay out salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know who Dragan Karna talked to, to organise the activities at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I think it must have been Milan Martic because nothing could be done without his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you observe any changes in terms of organisation as Captain Dragan arrived or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I was concerned, nothing changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Aside from training activities and instructors activities, did Captain Dragan get engaged in anything else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was this one action that he didn't take part in, really. No. He devised the whole action and then we carried it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, save for the training and the action at Ljubovo you say he planned, did you notice that Captain Dragan was engaged in any other activities as far as Golubic was concerned, the Ministry of the Interior, the Territorial Defence and anything else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Captain Dragan went about promoting himself extensively over the media. He talked a great deal. I think he was an eccentric. He had a high profile among the media. I didn't listen to what he had to say, really. He was extensively covered by the newspapers. He was engaged in self-promotion, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: A day after -- or, rather, following his activities in the training courses, this action, and his media appearances, did you observe him doing anything else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No. Aside from the training course intended for the police force and the reserve force at Golubic, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic. You said that in early June of 1991, you resumed your earlier regular policing duties in Benkovac. Who was your superior during your time in the public security station in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It was Chief Bosko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name, properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bakrac, I am stopping you here for just a second. The interpreters did not hear the name of the witness's superior while he was in the public security of Benkovac. Could you please ask him to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will repeat it, and the witness himself heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please slowly repeat the first and last name of your superior in the Benkovac police station.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Bosko Drazic was the chief of the Benkovac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, did you leave the police force in Benkovac at some point? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I left the Benkovac police force in late July because I clashed with Mile Martic. My colleagues who stayed behind in Croatia - in other words, stayed on the side of the Croatian police - signed an oath of loyalty, agreed to using the chequer-board symbol, and once these individuals were also chased out of police stations, they crossed over and came to join us in the Krajina. They were given jobs, although I opposed to working with individuals who, had they not been chased away by the Croats, would always have stayed there - in other words, they joined us because they were forced to - whereas Mile Martic rewarded them by giving them the same sort of jobs they had in the Croatian police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, when you say that you left the police force, did this mean that you simply left or you asked that your employment be terminated? How did this come about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I simply walked out of the police station. I didn't want to be a part of them any more. I didn't write any letters, any applications. I didn't feel that I needed to. I simply walked out of the police station and joined the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, Mr. Opacic, all of this happened in late July of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or rather, Your Honours, can we now look at P1212. The page is 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, this is a lengthy document. I will summarise it for you, and you'll tell us if you had occasion to look at the document during proofing. You'll also tell me now, for Their Honours and for the record, what your comments on this document are. The title of this document which has 11 pages is, "The Public Security Station in Benkovac." The disposition of posts in view of a new restructuring of the public security station in Benkovac. So we start with the various specialist service sectors, villages, and the individuals listed. The document doesn't have either a signature or a stamp, but it reads at the end that it was produced in Benkovac on the 18th of October, 1991. On page 9, under the Roman numeral III, it reads: "Special unit numbering 14 members." Under 1, we can read: "Goran Opacic." Do you recall me showing this document to you during proofing and reading it out for you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, tell me, mention is made here of some sort of a new organisation or structure of the 18th of October, 1991, and a special unit mentioned where, under 1, you're listed. In October of 1991, were you a member of the special police of the Benkovac police station?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, this does not reflect the truth at all and it can easily be checked in the archives of the secretariat of defence, because on the 2nd of October I took part in the action of disarming the Croatian population in Nadin. Already by that time I was a scout working for the Territorial Defence. So that was already the case in October. What was the date of the document again? The 18th or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The 18th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: This is not true at all. This may have been the case at the beginning of that year and then somebody simply copied the data onto this document. I left the police force in late July and transferred to the Territorial Defence. It was impossible for me to be both on the police and in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, I will ask my learned friend Mr. Groome. I don't think the document is under seal. Mr. Opacic, I will read this out for you, and these are names, and you will tell me if you were a member of a special unit with these people and if you know them: "Nikola Tintor, Sasa Matic, Jovo Uzelac, Milan Veselinovic, Ilija Vitas, Gojko Calic, Bozo Koncarevic, Dusko Tintor, Milos Rnjak, Bozo Miljkovic, Dusan Kresovic, Cedo Zecevic, and Zdravko Trkulja." Were you together with these individuals ever a special unit of the SJB Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: All these individuals you mentioned were with me working for the police station in Benkovac until I left the police force together with Dusan Kresovic. Again, that was in late July. Secondly, these individuals were with me in Golubic, too, during the time of Captain Dragan -- or, rather, before his time and during his time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I do understand where you say that you were with them in Golubic before Captain Dragan was there, but then you also said that Dusan Kresovic and you left this unit. What my question was, was if this was ever a special unit of any sort?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, this was no special unit. They were people -- for instance, Zecevic was assistant commander of the police station. We were never a special unit to speak of in the sense of going on intervention missions or something like that. And I was never in any of the actions together with these people save for Dusan Kresovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that it was only Dusan Kresovic who was with you. Now as for the individual under 14, Zdravko Trkulja. What was his duty in the police station?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I think he was the crime scene officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, let us look at a different document now. It was disclosed to us by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 2D1214. Your Honours, the document is currently being translated. What we need, however, is only the last page. There is a list of authorised officials there who worked in the Benkovac public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, this is what the text reads. The first three names are interesting. Yours is first: "Goran Opacic started on the 20th of February, 1991. On the 31st of October, 1991, transferred to the army." Let's stop here and let's ask you if this is true because you denied what the previous document said. Perhaps you can explain this.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, the first date of the 20th is correct. That's when I was in the police. But the second date is not true in so far that I did not transfer to the army but to the Territorial Defence. It had never crossed my mind to join the army. In fact, the army would imply the JNA, and I was never in the JNA. I didn't want to. I didn't want to join that army. Instead, I was a member of the Territorial Defence as a scout under the immediate command of Zoran Laci. This is something that you can check, if you can find their archives or their files. There was six or seven of us, scouts, and we were on their payroll.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said under the direct of command of Zoran. Can you repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Zoran Laci. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence for the municipality of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, the date of the 31st of October, 1991, is it correct? And if not, can you tell us why not and why would this document contain this date?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I don't know why the document reads this. My brother, Zoran Opacic, joined the army. I definitely did not. This is not true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Zoran Opacic is under 2 here. It reads for him that he started on the 2nd of March, 1991, and was there until the 30th of September, 1991, when he joined the army.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then from the 21st --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bakrac, I don't think we have the right document on the screen. My Serbian is not really great lately, but, nevertheless, I am under the impression that what we see here does not correspond to what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise because I said -- because the document has a lot of pages. It's still being translated, and I am looking at the last page which contains the list of names and dates, so I would just like to look at the last page of this document. I apologise, Your Honour, for not noticing that on the screen. The title is, "List of authorised officers who worked at the Public Security Station in Benkovac." There is no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, this is what I am interested in. Can you please just focus on my question. For Kresovic, Dusan, you say that he transferred to the TO together with you. On this list he's under number 3. It starts that he began on the 27th of February, 1991, and that he was at the Benkovac public security station until the 30th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct, because Dusan Kresovic left the police force at the same time as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you Mr. Opacic. If I understood you correctly, when in late July you transferred from the public security station in Benkovac, you went to the Territorial Defence; is that right? And which units did you -- which unit did you transfer to in the TO?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I went to the reconnaissance squad at the TO staff, and it was under the personal command of Zoran Laci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us how many men were there in this squad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Six to seven people, that was the core, and then there would be some other members joining from time to time who would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, at the time when you moved to the TO, what force was the TO part of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, it was part of the army. I suppose the Territorial Defence was part of the army. I didn't want to join the army, but I did want to go to the TO because it was all people who were from our area; people that you could trust, that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, Zoran Lakic, the commander of the Benkovac TO, who did he get his orders from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, he worked in agreement with the commander of the 180th Brigade in Benkovac. Cecovic, I assume --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch did last sentence by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And as part of the activities of the JNA, as a member of the TO, did you go into any action after you joined the TO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bakrac, I just have to interrupt you for one tiny second. The interpreters did not understand the end of the last answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, would you please be kind enough to repeat in your answer to my question if you knew from whom witness Zoran Lakic was receiving orders from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: He had to co-operate narrowly with the commander of the 180th Brigade, Cecovic, Trivko Cecovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I may help, I'm just going to repeat to check that I heard you correctly. Tripko Cecovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we will listen to it later because we don't want to lose time on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, in early October 1991, as a member of the TO, did you go into action with any unit of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: There was a decision made about working in co-ordination with the JNA, meaning the 180th Brigade. There was the Benkovac road, a highway leading to the airport. And there was a village there where there was constant fire on vehicles going down that road. Korlat, Biljane Gornje, Biljane Donje, Crljuge were -- and Zemunik Gornji were all hit by mortar fire. And then there was a decision made for an action in which I participated to disarm these people who were firing at Serb settlements and on the highway who were firing at military or civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And how did this action end? What happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: A platoon of the intervention unit, under the command of Slavko Draca, undertook that. We received two tanks and cruise from the 180th Brigade, but mostly it was our men from the reserve forces who were there. In this operation -- during this operation, one tank tripped a mine and the other tank, with me, Slavko Draca, and the rest of us who were on the other side of Glavica, we carried out our assignment successfully and we entered the Brzoja Varos village in the tank. A member of the forces, Boro Strbac, who belonged to the reconnaissance unit, was killed in combat with these Croats. What happened was that we managed to get there but the other ones couldn't get through because their tank hit a mine and there were people who were injured. At that point in time we were surrounded and exposed to fire by the enemy. We put up a defence and we asked Zoran Laci to call the military police company to help us. They were located in the Benkovac barracks and they were under the command of Major Ristic and Captain Milivoj Ostojic. So what happened next was that instead of coming to help us straight away, they took this military police company to the firing range in Glisici [phoen] and we waited for five hours for them to come and help us to get ourselves -- extricate ourselves from this situation. It took them a long time to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And how did you understand this, that you had to wait for help for so long from members of the 180th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I understood that as a betrayal, that they wanted as many of us to get killed as possible so that we would not present ourselves anymore as any kind of military formation because they wanted us to break apart because we would not accept to be under their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us how this event in Nadin reflected on the your relations with the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well the relations were bad anyway, but this was a culmination. I understood this to be a betrayal and that in a sly way they he worked for us to come to harm.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic. It's time for a break. I am looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very good idea. But just before the break, I would like to ask you to ask the witness to repeat. The interpreters did not understand what he just said, the very last answer. Maybe you could put the question to him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, just for the transcript so that your words would be recorded properly in the transcript, I asked you how this event in Nadin reflected on your relations with the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It was very bad. It was an act of betrayal, as if they wanted to liquidate me in a perfidious way, without directly participating but by allowing us to be exposed to fire. And for them to go to target practice while we are out there losing our lives, you understand, and they went to target practice and didn't want to come, and that was only 6 kilometres away from the Benkovac barracks. Did you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. It's clear now. Thank you, Mr. Opacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And then after the break, Mr. Bakrac, please let us know what you intend to do with the documents that you showed to the Tribunal. I don't know if you want to have them admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I am not mistaken, perhaps I did not refer to all three documents. No, I'm sorry. The first two documents have already been admitted, D117 and P1212, but 2D, the last document, I am going to just tender pending the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last one? So if I understand you correctly, you would like to have this document admitted and you would like it to get an MFI number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We did not manage to obtain a complete translation but we hope to do that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask that we reserve any objection we might have until we are able to read the document once the translation comes in. So if it's being marked for identification then it's -- that it's not simply about the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. It will be MFI'd for the two-above mentioned reasons. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1214 will receive number D765, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] MFI, very good. So we will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to mention that the witness got the authorisation not to stand up. He doesn't have to rise because there are many different cables around him, so he doesn't have to rise. Mr. Bakrac, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, before the break we talked about the misunderstanding you had with the army, if I can put it that mildly. This is my question: Did the JNA commence certain operations in early October to lift the blockade of its barracks, and if so, do you know where?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: In Zadar and Sibenik. I am sure about Zadar, though. There were three or four barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the course of the operation to lift the blockade of the barracks, were there attempts made to capture Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, was it in November that an attack was mounted on Skabrnja in order to neutralise the Croatian army that was stationed in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us the strategic importance of gaining control over Skabrnja? How many troops were there in Skabrnja, approximately, and what were their activities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly how many there were there. There were Skabrnja and Nadin, and there were two elevation points there which provided good vantage points. They kept on placing in danger, from these two vantage points, the road leading to the Zemunik airport, as well as the road leading from Benkovac, Biljane Gornje, Smijocici [phoen]. They fired from 120-millimetre mortars, for the most part. The main road passed along these two villages and they opened fire on the road from Nadinska Glavica elevation from infantry weapons. There were quite a lot of casualties. Civilians would also get killed from mortar shells that they fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In November of 1991, did there come a time when you received information of an attack being prepared on Skabrnja, and if so, who did you learn it from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when the day of the attack came, I didn't know that we were about to attack that location. It was on the eve, the evening before, that I received an order from my commander, Zoran Laci, that I should take a reconnaissance squad, complete with some five or six extra men, so there was the total of 12 of us, and that with a tank we should take Razina Glava [as interpreted] feature before the attack itself, which was supposed to take place from the Zemunik Gornji and then proceed toward the east, and that this was supposed to be carried out by the JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- do you know which forces were supposed to take part on the attack on Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It was a company of the military police, I believe. There was also the army there with APCs, that much I know. As for the rest, there were Territorial Defence members and some policemen. There were there as infantry men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know Aco Draca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was the head of the state security in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: A day before the attack on Skabrnja, did you happen to see Aco Draca in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: After hearing there Zoran Laci that an attack was to take place on Skabrnja the following morning, I met up with Draca because the TO staff had an office upstairs where there was an office of the state security of Benkovac as well. The police had their premises there as well as the court in Belgrade [as interpreted]. I spoke who Aco Braca about this, and following the negative experience from Nadin I was afraid that the army might set us a trap again with a view to having us killed during the action. It was with great reluctance that I set off on that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, let us clarify or correct the transcript. You said that the premises of the police were right next to the premises of the court in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You don't have to go on explaining because what was entered in the transcript was "the court in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, no. Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You were just telling us what you were discussing with Draca. When were supposed to set off on this assignment you received from Draca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to be on the location at 5.00, and my operation was scheduled to commence at 6.00. The same applied to the others. It was synchronised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you join this assignment that you received from Zoran Lakic after all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we got to Biljane Donje, this was our starting point, and from there we went in the direction of Skabrnja and Razina Glava feature. Tanks were there, they were supposed to provide support to us. We were supposed to capture Razovljeva Glava because it was a dominant feature. And once this was taken, we would be in control of the area. I agreed with the tank crew that the 12 of us would go ahead and should there be any land-mines in the area, we had an explosive specialist. We came across several mines, but they -- we managed to clear the area of them. We were some 800 metres away from Razovljeva Glava at that point. We got into a brushwood and fanned out, and at that point the tanks made a U-turn and went away. I was surprised by this development. I went back to one of the tank crew and he told me that their orders were to go back to the starting point and stay there. I immediately told the man that this was a betrayal. We said that we would no longer be part of this. We got into a car. We went to Biljane Donje, I abandoned my position and went to Benkovac. This was roughly 7.00 in the morning by that point. I spent the day in Benkovac. I think I even encountered Aco Draca and I told him what had happened up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's make this completely clear. If I understand you correctly, you set off from the starting point to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Razovljeva Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please wait for me to put the question to you. You set off from the starting point, and 100 metres into your journey the tanks turned around and at that point you aborted your mission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was indignant. I decided to abort the action. I didn't want what happened in Nadin to happen to me the second time around. I felt that we were being left in the lurch. I simply did not trust them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If you recall, can you tell us who was with you at the time? Can you give us a few names of those who were your group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Razic [as interpreted], Visic, Medak, Djokic, Rujak. We even had a journalist from Tanjug with us who took photographs of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic. Did you go back to Skabrnja or Nadin that same day or the day after? Did you go back to the area where there was fighting or did you never go back again?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: You see, there was fighting going on in Skabrnja for one day only. The next day I went to the village of Rujakova Kosa [phoen] in the vicinity there and there was nobody there. It was deserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say you went there, you went to Nadinska Glavica feature and there was no fighting going on any more?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: There were no combat activities going on on the following day. Besides, the army didn't even participate in the action on the second day. You see, there was fighting going on in Skabrnja on the first day; whereas, on the second day, both the population and the army left, and there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we look at P1208 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, while we're waiting for Their Honours and our learned friends to see the document, I will tell you that it is one of the documents we reviewed during your proofing. It's a document of the 180th Motorised Brigade. It was the security officer Major Bratislav Ristic who wrote a note on the 27th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page, which is page 5 in English and page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for Their Honours to review this, I will read out the explanation. It is a report on the killings of the civilians in Skabrnja. It is stated that on the 25th of December 1991 this security organ apparently got in touch with a collaborator who had some information about the killings of civilians in Skabrnja. And he goes on to say that he got the following information from this collaborator. "Goran Opacic came here today (a member of the special unit of the SJB Benkovac). In front of all of us in the office, he talked of how there were killings of civilians mostly women and old men in Skabrnja. Volunteer Chetnik, known as Jaro Jare (originally from the village of Prebilovac in Herzegovina) and his friend from the same unit, a man called Ljubisa, were practically prominent in these killings." Let me stop here and ask you is this: On the 25th of December, 1991, were you a member of the special unit of the Benkovac SJB at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, I was a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you discuss with anyone in the office or elsewhere the issue of there having been civilians killed, women and elderly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That's a pure fabrication. How would I be discussing something that I did not witness or participate in? It was common knowledge in Benkovac that I did not participate in this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know this Major Branislav Ristic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And were you on good terms with him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, we did not get on very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Because he -- I told you about the first attack in Nadin when he sent the military police company to target practice instead of sending them to help us. He sent them to the village of Listic [phoen] to target practice, and that military police company was directly under his control and under control of Major Ostojic. And so we considered them to be traitors and war profiteers and cowards because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, before we finish with this document, it states here as well that a certain Zoric -- Zoric, who was somewhere in the JTO, went around the town showing a bag full of human ears, and he entered the Seven [phoen] cafe bar and provocatively called the waitress to show her a dirty glass and when she came, he showed her a glass in which there was a human ear. This event with Zoric in the cafe, is that something that you know about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, there is no way. This is pure fabrication. There is no way anything like that could have happened. These are just pure lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Opacic, did Major Ristic ever come to see you, ask you or members of the unit who were there with you, did he ever try to talk to you about any of these things?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we look at the next document, please. This document was from the 27th of November, 1991. And the next document is P1209. And we are going to look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting, just this. Mr. Opacic, when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bakrac, while we wait for the document to be called up, I can see it now, how much longer will you be needing? You have told us that you need approximately an hour and a half for the examination-in-chief of the witness. I believe that the hour and a half are up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if nothing else, I have made a bad time estimate here. I do apologise. I discussed this with my colleagues from the Prosecution. Of course, you are the ones who decide on the time, but my learned friend Mr. Groome has said that he would back me up in my request for a little bit of additional time because as I have already said of my tendency to make bad estimates. But I believe that I could finish within the next 20 minutes to half an hour, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I can save Mr. Groome and back Mr. Bakrac up myself. I will only need around 10 to 15 minutes, so if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution estimates that it will use three hours. I expressed some concern with Mr. Bakrac because there were over 50 documents noticed to the prosecution that he would deal with. And it seemed to me that after the first session we had hardly made our way through it. But he is correct, I would not object to whatever the Chamber thinks is fair. I believe it's the only witness this week. I believe it's a rather important witness so whatever the Chamber thinks is fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Mr. Bakrac. The Chamber is allowing you to continue for 20 more minutes. You got your 20 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. And I apologise once again for my bad estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Opacic, Ostojic, Milivoj, he's the superior of the security organ, and we are looking at the official note of the 8th of March, 1992, so this is almost three months or more after this event. I am going to draw the Chamber's attention to the end of the first page. We will start at the bottom of the page. So where we have now Milivoj Ostojic of the security organ on the topic of Skabrnja, and he says the following --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have the English text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be no interpretation in any language whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Exhibit P1209. I think that you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very good. I think we have it. Indeed, yes, we have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, in this official note by Ostojic, what it says now is that Gnjidic was the one who was showing -- actually, earlier we saw Ristic saying that Zoric was showing this ear to the waitress and put it in the glass, and, now three months later, we see that Ostojic is writing that it is actually Gnjidic in a cafe showed an ear to a waitress, keeping it in a glass while telling her that the glass was dirty. Do you know about this event, that Gnjidic was showing any ear in a cafe anywhere?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I don't know this Gnjidic at all. I never seen him or heard of him. This Gnjidic was never in the unit with me. I don't know. Perhaps it's Zoric. It's Gnjidic. Perhaps they know who it is but I don't. But I think that this has nothing to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, I need to finish in the next 20 minutes or so, so I would just kindly ask you to focus on answering my questions. Thank you for your answer. We are now going to go back to the second paragraph which says that: "Volunteers from Serbia were killing in the village of Skabrnja while Opacic's group, according to unverified information, carried out the murder of the Odzakovic family members, Odzakovic the boxer, in the village of Nadin, and killed three prisoners in the villages of Skabrnja and the village of Smiljcic."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English, it's the end of the first and beginning of the second page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether this is true.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: This is a pure lie. For as long as I was in the war until the time I was wounded, it never happened that we struck a civilian, never mind that we killed anyone. I never saw this village of Odzakovic. I know about the village but I've never been there. I've never been to Skabrnja, so I don't know about the civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, this Major Milivoj Ostojic, did he ever discuss this incident with you, did he ever take a statement from you, or did he try to check with you or any of your associates any of these allegations here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And is this that same Ostojic for whom you said because of the events in Nadin that he and Ristic were war profiteers and traitors?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the military security service ever submit any charges against you for the allegations that I've read to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No. Neither the military nor the state security service ever submitted any criminal reports about this, anything like that. Nobody ever called me about that. I never saw anything like that. This is only, you understand, with them. There was state security service. They also had information. They knew who it was and what was going on. I mean, this was something that went on parallel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic. Can you please tells whether volunteers from Serbia were ever under your command, any volunteer from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, how long did you spend in this TO formation, until when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Until the UNPROFOR came, and then we were disbanded. We were on stand by for a while and then everybody went home. Once the UNPROFOR came, there were no more combat actions. There was no more need for anybody to be engaged. I was a free civilian again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I think it was about a month after the UNPROFOR arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what year is that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: This is 1992, I think, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And at what point in time in 1992 were you engaged in any actions, and, if you were, which action was this and who deployed you there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I was there in the action to break through the corridor. The police from Benkovac was engaged in trying to break through the corridor, but I was a free civilian at the time and guys were supposed to assemble -- people were out in the field for 15 days and they needed to be replaced, so the commander in Benkovac said to me that we needed to find some other guys, get together, and to go and relieve the guys who were deployed in the action to breakthrough the corridor. We went there and we were placed under the command of Milan Martic, and we completed our action successfully. And after that we returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you returned home, did you join any unit, any formation, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't join any formation. When I returned from the action in the corridor, I was in the office of Momcilo Bogunovic when the weapons and the equipment was being returned, the vehicles and so on. And then General Boro Djukic called, and he said, I don't want to see Opacic and his men in any formation. That is what he said, "in any formation."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. Let me just stop you here so that I could put a couple more important questions to you so that we use the time that we have. Momcilo Bogunovic, what was he at the time, and who was Boro Djukic at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Boro Djukic I think was in Knin. He was the main security person, a commander of the police over there, perhaps the army there. The officers who were there in the JNA, they moved then -- they transferred to the Krajina police force then. I think that he was a commander. I don't know exactly what he was. But since he was the main security person at the time in the Knin Corps area -- Boro Djukic, that's what he was, he was the number one security person in that area, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Momcilo Bogunovic, what about him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Momcilo Bogunovic followed Cecovic. He was the commander of the Benkovac barracks. When the Krajina police went there after the UNPROFOR came, the army went to Serbia and the officers who were from our area, who were securing that area, they stayed in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was established after, as you said, UNPROFOR arrived, the army -- the JNA left, and the military transferred into the police for a time. And then after a certain period of time, did -- was the Army of the Serbian Krajina, was it established?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: In late 1991, November or something, I cannot remember, the chief of the police, Slobodan Vojko, who was in Benkovac, and Momcilo Bogunovic stopped me on the street in Benkovac, and they told me, Goran, you are enjoying a good reputation among the people as a fighter from the front, and you have to join either the army or the police. You cannot just stand on the sidelines. And since I was in the police, the former JNA officers had left, so then I decided to join the police. The 92nd Brigade, the military police in Benkovac, whenever it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: This was in late 1992, early 1993. I think it was December 1992. I'm sorry. I don't know exactly the dates. It could have been November or December in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. Can you please just tell us this: At one point were you wounded, and if you were, just briefly tell us when and how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: There was an aggression by the Croatian formations. This was on the 22nd of January. Although we were under the protection of the United Nations they attacked us, and it seems that on the 22nd early in the morning we were attacked. The UNPROFOR did not let us pull our weapons out. And then at 6.00 in the morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, please. We don't need all the information about the action itself. We are short of time. You are -- when you say that you are talking about the 22nd of January --

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It was the 22nd of January at 5.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly your eyes were injured and you had to go for treatment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was shot in both eyes and I was blind for three months almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now I would like to hear two things from you: When was it that you saw Mr. Franko Simatovic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I saw Franko Simatovic perhaps once or twice. Once in front of the police station in Knin. He sported Ray-Ban glasses and he drove a red car with Belgrade registration plates. As far as I can remember, I asked people who he was and they told me that he was a security person from Belgrade, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that it was in Knin, when was that? What year? Can you tell us what month?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It was in 1991 and I believe that it was either in June or some time around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he wear a uniform or was he in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: He was in -- wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And his car, was that a passenger car or was that a police jeep?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It was a red passenger car. I don't know of what make, but it was a normal passenger car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After that, did you ever see Mr. Simatovic again?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Simatovic in 1997 during a ceremony of some sort?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him at the celebration of the special operation at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, could you please tell us whether you were ever a member of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia or its state security?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I was never a member of the state security of Serbia. I helped Zoran Rajic when he was setting up JSOs. Our lads who were there were to become members, and I helped Zoran Rajic with the training. He asked me to draw up the plan of the training of those new members.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, let us just correct something. If I understood you properly, in 1991 you saw Franko Simatovic in Knin, as you have described for us; and then in 1997, where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: At Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How did you find yourself there? Did you participate in that ceremony at Kula?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Zoran Rajic invited me, and my brother, Milos Opacic, was a member of the special operations unit, and Rajic is my family friend. He invited me the attend the celebration of that unit, and the lads that attended also hailed from my region. I knew them from before. They were linked to the unit. They were members of that unit, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you go to that celebration in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I arrived at that celebration wearing civilian clothes and that's how I returned, but there was a little surprise in store for me there. When we arrived there, I saw my old comrades, Svetozar Nakarada, Subotic, Zika Jovanovic, Olujic, Dula Orlovic, who was the head of security in Krajina. And there was a surprise in store for us. They told me personally that we had to put uniforms on because President Milosevic was supposed to arrive. We want to display you as war veterans. And from Zika Jovanovic bestowed -- bestowed on me the rank of colonel. And then I returned the uniform and the rank. So I was a colonel for about two or three hours, until the moment the ceremony ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And before that ceremony, did you ever see Rajo Bozovic or Milorad Ulemek or Vaso Mijovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Vaso Mijovic and Radojica Bozovic, I saw them for the first time. I knew Ziko Milovic [phoen], and I knew of Milorad Ulemek. He was Arkan's Men, and I didn't know him. I only heard of him and read about him. And he came to our region in 1993 when an attack was mounted on Ravni Kotari and the Maslenica bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, I am bringing my examination to an end. My time is running out. Kindly tell me again, did you ever, from 1990 up to the ceremony which took place in 1997 or even perhaps until today, were you ever an employee, an active duty employee or reserve duty employee, of the MUP of Serbia or the state security of Serbia?
