utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: What year? From 1990 until?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Until today.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you imply by that. I was preparing those lads for service. I drafted a plan for their deployment. And if you want to consider that as me being a member of that unit, then that is something else, but I was never a member of the state security. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that you were helping Zoran Rajic in drafting a plan and programme, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That was in 1996 and 1997 when our lads who had arrived from Krajina and who were considered candidates to join that unit for special operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to look at one document, 2D1213, and then I would end with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, when you were wounded on the 22nd of January, 1993, you were supposed to go abroad for a surgery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you receive any aid or assistance for that surgery? And if that was the case, who did that come from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I was operated twice in Belgium, in Antwerpen, by Relja Zivojinovic, and both of the operations were paid for by the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you provide us with a government decision dated 30 May 1993 where it says that the -- Djordje Bjegovic, the prime minister of the RSK, approved an amount of 10.000 German marks for your eye surgery?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this moment I would like to tender 2D1213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have until after the next break to discuss perhaps with Mr. Bakrac just some information about this document. It's -- we are unfamiliar with it, and then I'll state our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will been be admitted provisionally and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D213 will received number D716, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for giving me a -- some additional time. And once again I apologise for my bad estimate, and these were all the questions I had for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Opacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Jordash. Mr. Opacic, now you will be examined by Mr. Jordash, he who represents Mr. Stanisic in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't have many questions for you, maybe ten minutes or so. And I want to, in the ten minutes or so, just ask you about some evidence which was heard at the ICTY. First of all, I don't know if you're aware but Zoran Lakic gave evidence in the Martic case. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something he said and see if you have comments about it. This is evidence given on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There seems to be some problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, we can hear some music being played and there is also a telephone that rings?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Probably preferable to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's a bit calmer. We can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to just ask you if you can comment on some testimony that Lakic gave in the Martic case, on the 27th of October, 2006, at page 10224. And he was discussing the operation this Skabrnja, and I want to ask you if you agree or not with some of his comments. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 10224, Lakic said that the operation was launched against Skabrnja "with the sole aim of convincing the Croatian forces with peaceful means to allow the pullout of the technical -- of the military technical equipment smoothly and that was the sole reason behind the action." Was that your understanding of the object of the operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe that what Lakic said was correct, but there were also attacks mounted by the Croatian forces from the same place, and that was the main reason why things had to be done. I am sure that they did not allow for the weapons to be pulled out. They opened fire on those villages and actually threatened the roads leading to those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Some more testimony that he gave. Page 10247. He's asked the question at line 11: "Do you accept the possibility that members of the SAO Krajina police were present in the village before you arrived?" He answered: "I do not accept that for the simple reason that I know they were not active. Well, I know I wasn't along the axis of attack. That's true. However, the unit -- or, rather, I should say, police force, police patrols carried out those duties that were envisaged under the plan involving the peace agreement. They weren't there when I was there, nor were they there before on that axis." Do you agree with Mr. Lakic that the SAO Krajina police were not part of the Skabrnja operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: The SAO Krajina police? I never met them. There were military police and the members of the police there, from Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The question is more direct than that, Mr. Opacic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: In that sector, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Go ahead, finish your comment about the sector.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I don't know what units participated in all of that. I know that there were members of the military police -- or perhaps not the military police or some military. Lieutenant Stanojevic actually got killed there in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I might inquire. It seems that Mr. Jordash is reading from a transcript of another trial that hasn't been tendered in this case. So my query is: Is it his intention to impeach this witness with some evidence from another trial, or is he laying foundation to ultimately tender this testimony? It's unclear to me exactly the exercise we are undergoing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly not laying the foundation to introduce the evidence. It's really just to ask the witness about the evidence given by Lakic and see what he has to say about it, which is, as I understand it, consistent with what we have been doing during this trial, including what Ms. Marcus did last week when putting to a witness what other individuals had said at trials at the ICTY or what other witnesses had said to the Prosecution in interviews held by the Prosecution, which in many ways is a much less satisfactory mode of examination in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's not so much the procedure that I am objecting to, it's the purpose of it. Is it -- it seems to me that there are two traditional reasons for doing so: One is to refresh a witness's recollection, and I don't believe we have exhausted the witness's recollection at this stage; or, typically to impeach a witness, to suggest that perhaps their evidence is in error in some regard. I am just simply not sure what exactly is being done now by introducing or reading the transcript of a case that's not in evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I am asking the witness about -- as I have just said, I am asking the witness about the evidence and asking him what his view is and whether he agrees with it or not. If he doesn't agree with it and I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If he doesn't agree with it and it's part of our case, then I will then take the next step and impeach him. And, that's going to be a bit clearer in a moment because the witness gives a very clear indication that this witness wasn't present at Skabrnja but gives a different reason than what the witness has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept Mr. Jordash's representation and withdraw my objection. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Jordash. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, could you answer the question I put to you, which was: Do you accept that the SAO Krajina police were not part of the operation in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no. I wasn't there. I was not fully aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let me ask you about another comment Mr. Lakic made. Lakic says at page 10258 on the 27th of October, 2006, line 9: "To the best of my knowledge, a group, this Opacic's group, as it's called, certainly didn't take part in Skabrnja. I know at that at the time" -- Let me start that again: "... I know that at the time he was in Benkovac or, rather, outside the territory. And I say that with full responsibility because I happened to meet him myself, personally, when I was returning in the evening. And I know he didn't take part at all. Not only did he not take part, he could not have taken part." And then he goes on to say, on the same page: "Opacic was a professional policeman in the Croatian police, and as such -- well, that was his profession. He didn't have a group in any formal legal sense. He didn't have a unit. He didn't have a group. He didn't have a formation of that kind." And then further down the page: "He didn't take part in any operations that are being ascribed to him like the one in Skabrnja. I know that for certain because later on the police organs and the entire investigation and the results of it had to be sent to the commanders of the JNA. We had to report back to them." Did you have anything to do with this investigation, or were you aware of the results of the investigation sent to the commanders of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I had nothing whatsoever to do with that. I did go to see him -- actually, I was under his direct command. I stand by my statement that I already provided. I was supposed to take the elevation in Skabrnja but that means that I adhere by the same answer I provided in the previous statement. I was never in Skabrnja. I never participated in the operation there. I was supposed to participate but I did not and that was for the reason that I have already explained today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He then goes on to say, Mr. Opacic, at page 10263, when asked about -- well, let me put the question that was asked to him: "Did you hear anything about Goran Opacic bragging about killing civilians in Skabrnja? Did you ever hear anything about that?" And he answers: "I know Goran Opacic personally. This sort of bragging on his part is nothing new. He tried to oversell himself as a hero, but in actual fact he fled. He took to the hills whenever a situation was dangerous. In the opinion of the JNA soldiers, he was an average soldier, but one who was prone to telling stories. But I wish to say that he wasn't a member of the SUP Benkovac. He was a lone fighter." Mr. Opacic, is there any truth in that? Is that the reason you didn't take part in Skabrnja, because you fled?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: It's a lie. It's a lie. I didn't flee. I didn't want to participate in that operation. And when it came to the civilians, that had nothing whatsoever to do with that. That's a lie, a fabrication. He lies that I was not there. I received salary from the Territorial Defence staff in Benkovac. I was issued weapons from them, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Groome, may I ask you -- I believe that it's a good moment to take a break, but before that, I would like to ask you how much time will you need to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had originally given notice of three hours. I think it may be less than that, but I think I will be able to give a more accurate -- after I have had an opportunity to go through my notes, but in any case it will not be more than three hours. And may I suggest that during the break perhaps we check with the witness about his medical condition. It is clear that I will finish tomorrow morning, so if there is some medical problem that the witness -- that Mr. Bakrac referred to, perhaps that should be explored during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, we are going to contact our Registrar in Belgrade and ask them whether it is possible to -- for the witness to travel tomorrow afternoon. I think it should be possible. We shall take a break now, and we will start at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Opacic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Groome, who's the Prosecutor. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before I start, in the last session I had asked to have an opportunity over the break to consider our position with respect to D7 -- sorry, D766, marked for identification. I have done that and the Prosecution has no objection to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. D766 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, I want to be sure that we have a very clear understanding of your professional biography, and perhaps most significant for the Prosecution is if and when you worked for the state security department of the Serbian MUP. Do you, yourself, consider that you worked for the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, if you think that my helping Rajic prepare the lads who were over at our place to become members of the special operations unit, if that you consider to be co-operation with the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's not important what I think. What I am simply asking you is: While you were doing that, did you, yourself, consider that you were a member of the State Security Service? It seems by the way that you answered my question that you did not believe you were a member.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now can I ask you to please give us some more detail about this assistance that you provided to your friend, Zoran Rajic. Can you tell us with as much precision as possible when it was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Zoran Rajic helped me out when in 1995 my brother and I, who lived in Loznica after having fled, we were called by him to a place called Ilok in eastern Slavonia. He invited us to go and settle there because there were vacant houses there. We were also told that a unit of some sorts was going to be set up to defend eastern Slavonia. After having spent a month or two at Loznica, we moved to Ilok. Zoran Rajic, who was the commander of that unit, kept me listed as a member of that unit, although I was unable to do anything since I was disabled by that point. Still, I was listed to be a member of that unit in eastern Slavonia. There were roughly a hundred families who relocated to Ilok at that time. They were all individuals who had fled the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this first -- the time that you moved to Loznica, was the conflict still ongoing in 1995 or was this after the conflict had ended?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: You mean from Ilok or at the point when the republic of the Serbian Krajina fell? What do you mean? I am not clear in your question. What's the time-period you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps more simply, are you able to tell us the month in 1995 that you made this move?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: You mean the move to Ilok? Well, when the Krajina fell; in other words, on the 5th, or perhaps it may have been the 10th or the 11th. I don't know how long the journey took. At any rate, it was the month of August when the Krajina fell. We settled in a place called Brnjac, my brother Milos and I, together with my wife and child and my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you've said that Zoran Rajic helped you out by placing you on a list of a unit. Can I --

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- ask you, who did you believe Zoran Rajic was working for at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I thought that he worked for the Krajina security. I knew him at the time as a member of the Krajina security. I got to know him back in 1990 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know that because you told you that's who he worked for, or do you have that from another source?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I know him personally from the time of the road blocks. So our acquaintance lasted through to the war, and it was only in 1996 that he told me that he worked for the security of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when he told you that he worked for the security of Serbia, did he tell you when he fist began to work for the security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what was the purpose of putting you on a list of members of a unit that you say you, in fact, were not a member of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, after I fled the Krajina, I had no means of livelihood, either I, my wife, I had a child with her and she was pregnant, or my parents. So I was in a hopeless situation. Since we had been friends from 1990, he listed me as a member of that unit so that I would be able to receive funds on that basis and have something to sustain my family on. Secondly, he also took me along to the Tara river. He could have taken along anyone if he wished to, to train that particular unit. But he took me. Besides, this unit - and I will never forget this - they all gave up or forfeited their salaries and raised thousands of German marks in order for me to settle my housing problems, even though they, too, were refugees, didn't have a place to stay and had to feed their families, but I was in a precarious position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, would I be incorrect in characterising this as a fraud. As you representing and receiving payment for service to a unit that you, in fact, did not render service to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I was on the payroll, although I was not a member of the unit formally -- or, rather, formally I was but not in actual fact. I was wasn't present there. Zoran Rajic would bring along my salary, but I wasn't an actual member of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to be sure that we are speaking about the same person when you refer to Zoran Rajic, so can I ask that you be shown 65 ter 6428.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to the Registrar down below in Belgrade, it is tab 40 in the binder that we provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And sir, I am going to ask you to take a look at this photograph and then tell us two things: First, can you tell us whether it's clear enough for you to be able to reliable identify the two people in the picture. And then, if you can, tell us if you recognise them.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: This is Captain Dragan. And I believe this is Zoran Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it clearly, but I do believe that that is him. Yes. Captain Dragan and Zoran Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to see with any clarity the uniforms that they are wearing? And if so, can you tell us whether you recognise them and where are they from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, I can't see them clearly. Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you cannot see them clearly, I wouldn't want to ask you any further questions about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 6428, the photograph the witness was just shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I am not sure the purpose, really. There is no dispute that we are talking about the same Zoran Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that why you wanted to show him that photo, to make sure that it's the same Zoran Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am advised that it's not that uncommon a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add this: Could my learned friend, Mr. Groome, tell us the date when the photograph was taken? We don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure that it's really relevant to know when the photo was taken. If the only reason for which this picture is tendered is to make sure that it's the same Zoran Rajic as the one that we see on the photo with Captain Dragan, the objection, in fact, is slightly irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I withdraw my request if that is the only reason. I apologise, my comment has to do with the uniforms, but the witness did say that he was unable to comment on them anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jordash, let's not dwell too long on this problem. It doesn't seem to be such -- very serious problem, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, but I can see -- just to back up Mr. Bakrac, I can see the Prosecution waiving this photograph in the future and saying, Look at how great friends they were, and look how this connects Rajic, Dragan and the accused. I can see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I give Mr. Jordash my assurance that I will never claim that they are great friends, will he withdraw his objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The objection is overruled. The photo will be admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, under what Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6428 will receive number P3098, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So P -- I am not sure that the number is the right number, the number in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P3098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. P3098 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, I am going to ask you that you look at one other photo. It is 65 ter 1180.3, and is a photograph from a still of P2160, a video that is in evidence. I believe it has just been sent down and printed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the Registrar will find it in the document that he received over the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] With all due respect, Mr. Groome, this 65 ter is 1180.3, as indicated, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar in Belgrade, your intervention has not been recorded, but it is the right photo, indeed, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could ask the that the witness be given an opportunity hold it and examine it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not clear on who is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you're unable to, with any degree of reliability, identify the people, then I'd ask you not to do so. But if you think you can, then please do.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I cannot recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask: Is that because you are unable to see the picture clearly enough because of your eyesight; or you can see it clearly. You simply do not recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I can't see or recognise anyone because it's all very hazy. I can't see a clear image of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's leave it there. I will investigate whether we can send down a clearer picture. Now, if we could return to the work that you did for Mr. Rajic, I believe you said in 1996/1997, and that was the plan for deployment, could I ask you to tell us with as much precision as possible when you began that assistance or when you first gave that assistance?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: You mean the fitness training and all that? Well, I was involved in that back at Golubici under the command of Dragan Karne. I had prepared physical fitness course for our members --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the last bit the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few problems. First of all, the interpreter did not quite understand what the witness just said. And Mr. Bakrac, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In line 11, it was misinterpreted what the witness said. The witness mentioned a different name, that he was involved in a fitness training programme in Golubic under the command of ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat? We didn't hear what he said, the first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Opacic, could you please repeat very slowly and clearly the name of the person, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the command of Dragan Karna, that was when I arrived in Golubic and I was working with the lads who were there. That was back in 1991 in late April. And then I continued all the way to the point when I left Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm in fact--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm in fact drawing your attention to another period of time. You mentioned in your testimony earlier today that you assisted Zoran Rajic by drafting a plan for deployment of the JSO in either 1996 or 1997. Do you recall giving that evidence earlier today?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That's not how I put it. I said that I helped him out with the plan for the physical fitness programme of the candidates for the JSO, and that was in 1996 and 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that the only assistance that you gave Mr. Rajic was helping him develop a plan for improving the physical fitness of the candidates for the JSO?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did it take you to develop that plan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't take long for me to do that. When it comes to physical fitness programmes, I was an expert and I didn't require more than a few days for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I had to think of some machines that would be used with weights, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did you do this work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I did that on mount Tara near Bajina Basta in the hotel called Tara.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during the course of this work, did you ever visit the Kula centre, the Rade Kostic centre, to look at the facilities that were there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No. That was the work I did at Tara only, whereas I visited Kula only on the occasion of that particular celebration. And Rajic was there as well. And I had never been at Kula either before or after, although my brother worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you paid for this work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I did say that I received some sort of remuneration for it, and I did say that the other men forfeited some of their pay in order that I may be able to acquire for myself, my wife and my child, and in 1997 my other daughter was born. They raised basically to 20.000 German marks and that required them to forfeit their -- one of their monthly pays to raise that amount of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, is it your evidence that you were -- you received 20.000 Deutschmarks as compensation for having spent a couple of days developing a physical training course? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No, no. That is not my evidence. I did receive my regular pay, whereas this was just a humanitarian action on their part. Because I had been wounded and my sight was ruined, they raised this money for me for humanitarian purposes. I didn't get 20 German marks in exchange for my work on preparing this fitness plan. That would have been ludicrous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we simply focus on the payment for the fitness plan. Do you remember how you were paid? And if you remember, how much you were paid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well it was in dinars, but I can tell you that it was the equivalent of 800 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you receive that from Mr. Rajic or from someone else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I received the money from Mr. Rajic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if we can return to the first time you saw Mr. Simatovic. Can I ask you again, with as much precision as possible, to tell us the month and year that you recall seeing him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I did tell you this once already. I saw Mr. Simatovic outside of the police station, if I remember correctly. I am not sure where I saw him the second time, but I am sure that the first time I saw him was outside the police station in Knin. He drove a red car, a passenger car, with Belgrade license plates. I asked the people around who this was and they told me that he was a security guy from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the -- are you able to tell us how much time approximately elapsed between the first time you saw him in the Knin area and the second time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it was some three days later that I saw him. Perhaps he was in his car or passing through Knin. I can't be sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you speak to him on either occasion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I had never spoken to him. Not until I came to attend the celebration when that -- there was a review of that unit in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac has referred to a video, P61, of that celebration. Can you tell us -- we know what's on the video, can you tell us, did you have any interaction with Mr. Simatovic that we -- was not filmed? Did you have any conversation with him? Did you discuss any topics with him on the day that you were in the Kula centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: When the celebration ended, there was a memorial museum there where various artefacts were exhibited and that was where we exchanged a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you talk about, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, not much. He asked about my health. He had heard that I was wounded so he wanted to know how I was fairing and where I was living.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how long did you speak with him at this time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: A minute or two, perhaps. There was commotion. He had many other obligations. There was the President Milosevic there with the entire delegation. He didn't have time to talk to me. We -- it's not like we had been socialising from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do I understand your evidence correctly that the entire interaction that you have had over the course of your life with Mr. Simatovic is the one minute where you exchanged some conversation in Kula in 1997? Do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you questions in a similar vein with respect to Mr. Stanisic. Have you ever had over the course of your life any personal direct interaction with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Only at the point when he handed over some sort of a gift to me at this celebration. It was a knife for the sacrifice that I gave during the war. That was the once. And then I saw him on TV -- actually, I heard about it when UNPROFOR was in Bosnia and that whole affair, and that was when he appeared in public. Other than that, you couldn't see him easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that the only direct interaction you have ever had with Mr. Stanisic is when he gave you a gift of a knife in Kula in 1997?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You still maintain that you are not a member of the state security special units; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were other people who were not members of the State Security Service also given gifts during the ceremony in Kula in 1997?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who the recipients were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions and clarify some of your answers that you gave to Mr. Bakrac during your direct evidence. I want to return to the point where you were speaking about your special unit. And it's at transcript page 13 today. You said the following: "And this special unit of ours was well-equipped. We had double uniforms. We were paid more than regular members. We had Hecklers with silencers, machine-guns, sniper rifles. We had chemical tear-gas bombs and other devices." My question to you is: First, how did the equipment you have compare to the equipment in the possession of other Territorial Defence units and the newly formed police stations or police personnel?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: You must have misunderstood me. I spoke about the time when I was a member of the police during the existence of the state of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. I was a member of the special units of the MUP of Croatia in Zadar and Sinj and that is what I referred to. You must have misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Obviously I have. Thank you for correcting me. Now another -- other evidence you gave earlier today relates to a decision of Mr. Martic, and the question was: "And what you're saying now, is that a decision of Mr. Martic before Captain Dragan came or not?" And your answer was: "This was his decision that pre-dated the arrival of Captain Dragan. I came to Golubic based on that decision." My question to you is: What do you know about that decision? Can you tell us what you understood that decision to contain?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in 1991 when Plitvice was attacked, we wanted to form a serious unit composed of police members, and that's when Martic sent a dispatch to the Benkovac SUP, Obrovac [Realtime transcript read in error "Obudovac"], Gracac, Knin, Lapac SUPs, and invited all those who had left their previous police stations in Croatia to join. And they all came to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, or to be more precise the SAO Krajina. This means that we gathered there pursuant to his order in order to establish that unit which would be able to intervene at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting. Just to avoid confusion. In the transcript after "Benkovac" I am reading "Obudovac," which is not what the witness said. Could he be invited to repeat what he said after the Benkovac SUP? That's on line 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police station that belonged to the municipal organs of the interior in Benkovac, not in Obudovac. I did not say Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Opacic, you mentioned a few places. You talked about the SUP of Benkovac and then you also mentioned Obudovac and Gracac and Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obrovac. Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This is exactly what we wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the interpreters are requesting that you speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, Obudovac is not a place that has been mentioned frequently in this trial. Can I ask you to spell it so we can be sure that we have the correct spelling on the record.

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Obrovac. O-b-r-o-v-a-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now today at transcript page 17, you spoke about Captain Dragan and you expressed your opinion that you thought he was eccentric, that he was promoting himself extensively over the media, and that you didn't listen to what he had to say really. My question to you is: To the extent you heard statements made by Captain Dragan, did you consider the statements to be truthful and accurate about whatever the matter was that Captain Dragan was discussing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Captain Dragan used to exaggerate everything. He bragged a lot. He used to brag about himself to make himself more -- as popular as possible with journalists, with the media, with television journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us a concrete example, if you recall, of an example where he exaggerated something that you knew not to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: He talked about Knindza, about their capabilities. That's what he made up, Knindza, portraying them as invincible warriors and stupid things like that. He was the one who Knindza. Some wolves, some bears, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that he was describing units that did not exist, or he was attributing to some units that did exist qualities that they did not possess?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it -- I expressed two possibilities. Are you saying that both are correct, that he both invented units that did not exist and attributed false characteristics to ones that did?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: There were -- there were units, they existed, but he attributed to them those qualities that they did not possess.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now today at transcript pages 29 to 30, you were talking about Skabrnja and Nadin, and you described two elevation points that provided good vantage points. Have I correctly understood your evidence to be that these vantage points were controlled by Croat force and the object was to take those vantage points from the Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Those were Naviskovo Glavica [as interpreted] and Razanovo Glava [as interpreted]. They were both held by the Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in my understanding that both of these locations are outside the town centre -- centres of both Skabrnja and Nadin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Razanovo Glava, as far as I can remember, is between Donje Biljane village and Skabrnja, to the north of Skabrnja in the direction of Donje Biljane; maybe 2- or 300 metres from Skabrnja and over perhaps 400 metres from Skabrnja, and about 800 metres from the other village. And the Nadinska Glavica is west of Nadin -- actually, Nadin is on its western slopes and Rujakova Kosa is on its other side, on its northern side. Again, the latter village is on the slopes of this Nadinska Glavica hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registrar down in Belgrade to look at tab 1 of the binder provided by the Prosecution. This is a copy of P41.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And sir, this is a map. Again I would ask you to look at it. And if you think after looking at it that you can reliably mark the location of Razovljeva Glava and Nadinska Glavica, then tell me and then I will instruct you further on how I'd ask you to mark the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And perhaps it might assist those of us here if we can display P41 in court so that we can see what the witness is looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very difficult for me to see those elevations. I can't find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court, could I ask that the witness be allowed to hold onto the map overnight to see if perhaps he is able -- with some time able to study it. It's an unmarked map of P41 of the Skabrnja area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have got it. I think that this is Razovljeva Glava. This is Razovljeva Glava, but I don't know where Nadinska Glavica is. I believe that I have found Razovljeva Glava, but I am still looking for Nadinska Glavica and I am still unable to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Groome, is this in dispute, the fact that those villages are on the map? I can see it if I look at the map. And if I blow it up on my screen I can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I did not explore this with my colleagues on the Defence, but if they agree that the two elevations that were held by Croat forces were outside the town centres of both Skabrnja and Nadin, then there is no need to proceed any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it's going a little too far, don't you think, to conclude it that way because you are asking him to pin-point on a map places that are there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I think that perhaps we can rely just on the markings of the map. From looking at the map it's not clear exactly how large those areas are, but perhaps we will deal with that in another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, even if he says where these places are, it doesn't necessarily mean that those were the places where the Croat forces were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. I was simply trying to clarify his evidence about where they were. His evidence earlier today was that they were on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. But as you can see it's a little difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I withdraw those questions. And there is no need for the witness to work with the map any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I can now go to something that you gave in your -- some evidence that you gave in your direct testimony in response to a question that you were asked by Mr. Bakrac. It's at transcript page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC SAID
utterances.text: "Mr. Opacic, when you say that you left the police force, did this mean that you simply left or you asked that your employment be terminated? How did this come about?" You said: "I simply walked out of the police station. I didn't want to be part of them anymore. I didn't write any letters, any applications." My question to you is: Did you consider that you had abandoned your post?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I knew that as soon as I left I would never return. There was nobody to write to in order to get permission. I left the police of my own will, to put it that way, very simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now a little later or shortly after you gave that evidence, you were discussing your relationship to the command of the JNA, and you said the following at transcript page 26. Question: "And how did you understand this, that you had to wait for help for so long from members of the 180th Brigade?" Answer: "I understood that as betrayal, that they wanted as many of us to get killed as possible so that we would not present ourselves anymore as a kind of military formation because they wanted us to break apart because we would not accept to be under their command." Now I want to focus in on the last portion of your answer. When did you express to members of the 180th Brigade that you and your men would not accept to be under their command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: You certainly meant 180th, not 108th. That's the first thing I would like to mention. I did not have any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So how would they have known that you would not accept to be under their command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: They knew it because I did not -- you see, I did not sport a five-pointed star on my forehead. I sported the insignia of a cross with four Ss and then the Serbian "sajkaca," hat, the Nemanjic's hat. And they didn't like that. It was contrary to what they believed in. And I am sure that you will be able to find photos depicting me wearing those insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it true that you, in fact, did not accept to be under the command of the 180th Brigade of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I never wanted to be under their command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed to remove his hand from his mouth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please try not to put your hand in front of your mouth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, let me ask you then the next question: If you didn't want to be under the command of the police, and you did not accept the command of the army, who did you -- did you consider yourself to be under the command of anyone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I was under the command of Zoran Laci in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that you are --

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence, in a time of conflict, comes under the command of the army, does it not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Officially, the Territorial Defence was under the command of the military. But the military was composed of the officers who belong to the Albanians, as well as the Croats, Bosniak Muslims, and the Serbs. That was the composition of the command cadre. Whereas the Territorial Defence units were composed of the local officers from Benkovac and the region, which means that the officers were locals. I did not want to be commanded by some Albanian or some Croat or some Muslim. I did not want them to lead me into an operation against the Croatian Armed Forces or some such force. I didn't want to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can turn our attention to your time in Golubic. During the time you were in Golubic, did your brothers Milos and Zoran also participate in the training at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: My brother Milos was in the military in 1991, which means that he was discharged in 1992. He was a member of the Guards Brigade in Belgrade. My brother Zoran was an artillery man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were either of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, once again you're covering your mouth with your hand, and so it's a bit difficult to hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was either of your brothers present in the Knin area at any time that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: My brother Zoran was with me. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honours. I wanted to react before the witness answered. On line 3, it says that his brother Zoran was an artillery man but the witness's words were not properly recorded. Not everything that he said was recorded. Could perhaps Mr. Groome repeat his question and clarify with the witness where his brother Zoran was?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Opacic, could I ask you to again tell us where your brother Zoran Opacic was stationed and with what unit, if he was part of a unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: He was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he, Zoran Opacic, with you in Golubic during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was with me in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to yourself, do some of the people that know you also refer to you as Klempo, K-l-e-m-p-o?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And with respect to your brother Milos, is he also known as Ciroki, C-i-r-o-k-i, Ciroki?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, while he was at the Alpha centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did the training at Golubic last?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I was in Golubic for 20 days for the training when Captain Dragan came, if that's what you were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I am going to ask you whether you recognise any names and whether you recognise them as people that were also present at Golubic. Do you recognise the name of Dragan Oluic, O-l-u-i-c?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Dragan Oluic, the last name is familiar. Not the first name, though. Perhaps he's from Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you whether you recognise the name Davor Subotic, also known as Riki?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Davor Subotic, Riki. I think that he was in Golubic for the training, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was he one of the people being trained or was he one of the people conducting the training?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: When I was there, I don't think that he was there. He was not an instructor. He wasn't a policeman at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How do you know him then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: We met in the different fronts. He's from Obrovac. It's the neighbouring town next to ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what unit did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I think that he was in the Obrovac one because he was from Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How about a person by the name of Milenko Popovic, also known as Luj, L-u-j?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I don't know him. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you did you first meet Zivojin Ivanovic, also known as Zika Crnogorac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: The first volunteer who came to Golubic, that was him, and this was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to show you a video now. Before I do, let me ask you: Do you recall attending a celebration marking the two-year anniversary of the log revolution on 17 August, 1992, in Bukovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I gave a speech then in Bukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Bukovic is a village located in the Benkovac municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Correct. This was an anniversary celebration of the SDS in Bukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were Zdravko Zecevic and Arkan also present at that gathering?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Zdravko Zecevic was there as the president of the municipality and he was in the Benkovac SDS and he gave a speech. And then Arkan came. He also spoke. And General Boro Djukic also, and he also addressed the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You just said that you gave a speech. I am going to play --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am going to ask that we play 65 ter 6431, and I am going to ask that the Registrar down there confirm that he can see the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that it be played, and then I will ask you some questions afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I welcome you here, on this spot from which we ventured into our first actions, where we gathered when we left Zadar with the rifles we had stolen from the Ustashas down there. Where were the generals then? Where were the JNA officers? Why did they not defend their people then? Instead, they were looking into who would go where, whether the majority would be here or there, whether the old Yugoslavia would remain or would we go to Serbia. However, when they saw that the people were going towards Serbia, as this is the Serbian people, always has been and always will be ... and no Ustasha will ever defeat us. "And now that we have to make our own army, brown-nosers and fat cats are sucking up to us ... "As well as lazy bums and other incompetent persons who will lead these people into disaster. But we will not let that happen! Isn't that right, we will not allow it? "Believe me when I say that we are the force that will defend this people. Believe us! There is no special status. We can have the special status only over our dead bodies, only over our dead bodies. "We went to Zadar to get furniture out for the generals and flower pots, and we got slapped by the Ustasha. They humiliated us. But we could have conquered Zadar, Biograd. We would have had the Serbian sea and our own port now. And they are making fool of us again. "And do not throw your weapons away, because as long as the Ustasha, the Muslims and others, are our neighbours, let us not trust them ever. They will come at night and cut our throats. "We should never trust them, as long as we have neighbours like this. We could have given them a special status and not the other way around. But you see where we are at. They are giving us a special status. We also have to feel ashamed because our own Ustashas betrayed us. But there are still some. They are sucking up to UNPROFOR where we hid some cannon or a tank. We must kill such people on the spot! "And every rifle that has been oiled and is now kept under the pillow of every man. He is able to be at the position in ten minutes. But as long as this one from the warehouse, from this UNPROFOR, from these Ustasha ... as people say - trust no one but yourself! Long live the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is that you that we've seen giving that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Groome, can you please -- maybe you can ask the witness to see if he saw the video? I am not sure that he was able really to see the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, were you able to see that video?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: I did hear it, yes. And I recognised myself. It's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did it accurately record the speech that you gave on this occasion in Bukovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: From beginning to end. From beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want you to ask us or assist us in understanding some of what you said. At the beginning of your speech, you state: "I welcome you here, on this spot from which we ventured into our first actions, where we gathered when we left Zadar with the rifles we had stolen from the Ustasha down there." What are the first actions that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: The barricades, the log revolution that happened. At the barricades --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: -- there are no actions, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you use the phrase "we gathered," who else did you gather with? Who is the group that you are describing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: The people were there who were manning the barricades. I was at the barricades already in 1919, Biljani Gornji and the other village. The barricades were there manned by the inhabitants of the villages where the barricades were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you refer to rifles that you had stolen, where were the rifles taken from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: These were rifles that we took from the police station in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You continue by stating: "Where were the generals then? Where were the JNA officers? Why did they not defend their people then? Instead they were looking into who would go where. Whether the majority would be here or there. Whether the old Yugoslavia would remain or would go with Serbia. However, when they saw that the people were going towards Serbia, as this is the Serbian people, always has been, always will be ... no Ustasha will ever defeat us." When you say "people were going towards Serbia," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: When the conflict had begun between us and Croatia, the -- when the HDZ came to power, when the barricades first started, the conflict actually started already in World War II during the Ustasha regime, and they were intending to do that also in 1991 when we erected the barricades. The Croatian army was creating a kind of buffer zone -- or the JNA was creating a kind of buffer zone, but they knew that they were arming themselves in Croatia, so we took up our own defence. We were trying to save our lives from the Ustasha knives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Towards the end of the speech, you state: "We must kill such people on the spot." Who are you suggesting must be killed on the spot?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: When the UNPROFOR came, then our army - which was the army of the Krajina at the time - had some weapons concealed, self-propelled weapons and things like that. And some of them would go there and they would say where such a cannon was hidden or a rifle, and then the UNPROFOR would come and they would confiscate these weapons ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the rest of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we can hear your answer up until the point where you say that "UNPROFOR would confiscate these weapons." Can you please repeat again the remainder of your answer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN OPACIC
utterances.text: Those people who betrayed the places where the weapons were, who gave them away. And they were the inhabitants there. Also, I don't know for what reason they disclosed the places where the weapons were being hidden, and they were telling UNPROFOR that. And I said that those people should have been killed. And to this very day, I stand by that, that every single one of those people should have been killed for weakening the -- the combat strength of the Serbian people in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it's 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I was just going to mention it as well. It seems that the video that we just saw is not in the system. The Registrar tells me that it's not uploaded. If you wish to have it tendered, you will have to first upload it in e-court, and we can see about it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will check into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing stands adjourned up until tomorrow morning, Wednesday, March 14, at 9.00 in this same courtroom. And, Witness, I must instruct you not to discuss with anybody your testimony. Up until tomorrow morning, of course. You may not speak about it with anyone. And I wish you a good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
